guide.title: Prospect Lefferts Gardens, Brooklyn: Covenanted Blocks and Nostrand Avenue
guide.intro: The Lefferts family reached Flatbush in 1660 with Leffert Pietersen Van Haughwout, a Dutch immigrant, and by 1790 the family held seven enslaved people, with one member owning ten by 1810, in a county that had the highest proportion of enslaved people in New York State in the mid-1700s. In 1893 James Lefferts subdivided part of the family farm into roughly 600 building lots and attached perpetual covenants: single-family houses of brick or stone, at least two storeys plus a cellar, set back at least fourteen feet from the street, and costing a minimum of $5,000 to build. That is Lefferts Manor. The neighborhood's own name is much younger, coined in 1968 from Prospect Park, Lefferts Manor and the Brooklyn Botanic Garden.

sections.heading: A covenant, two districts, and Nostrand Avenue
sections.body:
Development here was spurred by the completion of Prospect Park, the opening of the Brooklyn Bridge and the arrival of mass transit in the late 19th century. The first residents were overwhelmingly middle-class professionals, businessmen, doctors, lawyers, brokers and clerks, many of them with domestic servants. The Lefferts Manor Association was founded in 1919, and still enforces the one-family-dwelling covenant and organises neighborhood events; it runs an annual self-guided house and garden tour through the district's blocks in late May, billed in 2026 as its 52nd.

The Landmarks Preservation Commission designated Prospect-Lefferts Gardens a historic district on October 9, 1979. Two smaller adjacent districts followed, Ocean on the Park in 2009 and Chester Court in 2014. The Lefferts Manor Historic District, 667 contributing rowhouses and freestanding houses built between 1896 and 1952, was added to the National Register of Historic Places on May 18, 1992, with a boundary increase listed on November 9, 2017; a broader Prospect Lefferts Gardens Historic District was added to the National Register on June 30, 2023.

Chester Court is the smallest and strangest of them: eighteen Tudor Revival rowhouses built in 1911 and 1912 by the Brooklyn architect and developer Peter J. Collins, arranged around a private cul-de-sac closed off from the Brighton subway line by an original brick wall, and styled after the black-and-white buildings of Chester in England.

One house is missing from all of this. The Lefferts family homestead, an 18th-century Flatbush farmhouse, originally stood at 563 Flatbush Avenue near Maple Street, inside what is now the neighborhood. It was moved into Prospect Park in 1918 and is preserved there as the Lefferts Historic House museum, which the Prospect Park Alliance lists as open in July and August, Wednesday to Sunday and holidays.

Since the 1960s Caribbean immigrants have substantially shaped the neighborhood, which overlaps with the area branded Little Caribbean along the Nostrand Avenue corridor. Allans Bakery, Aunts et Uncles and Caribbean Vibes all sit on that stretch of Nostrand.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Two subway lines reach the neighborhood from opposite sides.

On the IRT Nostrand Avenue Line, along the eastern commercial spine, Sterling Street at Sterling Street and Nostrand Avenue and Winthrop Street at Winthrop Street and Nostrand Avenue are both in Prospect Lefferts Gardens, and both are served by the 2 at all times and the 5 on weekdays.

On the BMT Brighton Line to the west, Parkside Avenue at Parkside and Ocean Avenues serves Prospect Lefferts Gardens and Flatbush, and is served by the Q. Prospect Park station, at Empire Boulevard and Flatbush Avenue, is served by the B, the Q and the Franklin Avenue Shuttle; its source describes it as serving Flatbush, Prospect Lefferts Gardens and Crown Heights, and places it near the border of Crown Heights.

Buses run along both commercial spines: the B41 on Flatbush Avenue to the west and the B44, local and Select Bus Service, on Nostrand Avenue to the east.

faq.question: How do I get to Prospect Lefferts Gardens?
faq.answer: Sterling Street and Winthrop Street, both on Nostrand Avenue and both in the neighborhood, are served by the 2 at all times and the 5 on weekdays. On the Brighton Line, Parkside Avenue at Parkside and Ocean Avenues has the Q, and Prospect Park station at Empire Boulevard and Flatbush Avenue has the B, the Q and the Franklin Avenue Shuttle. The B41 runs on Flatbush Avenue and the B44 on Nostrand Avenue.

faq.question: Where does the name come from?
faq.answer: It was coined in 1968 by the Prospect Lefferts Gardens Neighborhood Association, combining three landmarks that border the area: Prospect Park, Lefferts Manor and the Brooklyn Botanic Garden. Lefferts Manor is itself named for James Lefferts, who subdivided the family farm into roughly 600 covenanted building lots in 1893.

faq.question: Can I visit the Lefferts family farmhouse?
faq.answer: Yes, but not in the neighborhood. The homestead originally stood at 563 Flatbush Avenue near Maple Street and was moved into Prospect Park in 1918. It is preserved there as the Lefferts Historic House, run jointly by the Prospect Park Alliance and the Historic House Trust, and the Alliance lists it as open in July and August, Wednesday to Sunday and holidays.

photos.description: A brick end-of-row house with a tiled gable, half-timbering and an ivy-covered flank wall, on a Prospect Lefferts Gardens street.

places.name: Lefferts Manor Historic District
places.address: Roughly an eight-block area around Lincoln Road, Fenimore Street, Rogers Avenue and Flatbush Avenue, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: 667 contributing rowhouses and freestanding houses built between 1896 and 1952 under the deed covenants James Lefferts attached to the land in 1893. An area to walk rather than a single site.
places.history: The district was designated by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission on October 9, 1979, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on May 18, 1992, with a boundary increase listed on November 9, 2017. The Lefferts Manor Association, founded in 1919, still enforces the one-family-dwelling covenant.

places.name: Chester Court Historic District
places.address: Chester Court, a cul-de-sac off Rogers Avenue, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: Eighteen Tudor Revival rowhouses arranged around a private cul-de-sac, closed off from the Brighton subway line by an original brick wall and styled after the black-and-white buildings of Chester, England.
places.history: The houses were built in 1911 and 1912 by the Brooklyn architect and developer Peter J. Collins, and the court was designated a New York City historic district in December 2014.

places.name: Allans Bakery
places.summary: A Caribbean bakery on the Nostrand Avenue Little Caribbean corridor, known for rolls, patties and desserts. City health department records show it inspected at this address in June 2026 with a Grade A.

places.name: Aunts et Uncles
places.summary: A plant-based cafe on Nostrand Avenue serving Ital, the Rastafarian vegetarian cuisine, along with cocktails and cafe fare. Its own account posts hours of Sunday to Wednesday, 10am to 8pm.

places.name: Caribbean Vibes
places.summary: A Caribbean restaurant and bakery on Nostrand Avenue serving oxtail, fish and curry dishes. City health department records show it inspected at this address in July 2026 with a Grade A.

links.note: Prospect Park forms the neighborhood's western border, and the Lefferts family homestead was moved into it in 1918.
Prospect Park station, near the border of Crown Heights, is described as serving Flatbush, Prospect Lefferts Gardens and Crown Heights.
Both neighborhoods' commonly cited boundaries run along New York Avenue, and Brooklyn Community Board 9 covers both.
The neighborhood's name was coined in 1968 from Prospect Park, Lefferts Manor and the Brooklyn Botanic Garden.
